source.title: Partially Rewriting a Transformer in Natural Language

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether natural-language explanations of sparse features predict activations on new contexts well enough to preserve model behavior; the reported performance is close to zero ablation, with strong dependence on calibration.
record.gate_note: The study measures simulated activations and resulting next-token loss for sparse transcoder and SAE features. The cited neuron-explanation studies and their results are background only. Figure-based values without textual numerical reports are not transcribed as numbers.
record.test_reason: This study does not test any version. It scores natural-language explanations of sparse transcoder and residual-SAE latents trained on Pythia 160M, not the model's own neurons, so the unit of analysis is a different construct. V6 and V7 concern explanations of neurons. The finding that latent explanations fail to predict activations (about 80% specificity, loss near zero ablation) is related, so it goes under fits_no_version. Polysemantic neurons come up only as background in the introduction. This is a judgment call: the transcoder is described as an MLP with sparsely activating neurons, but it is a trained replacement and not the network's own units.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that current latent explanations are too unspecific and produce many false positives. Without quantile normalization, even 20% of latents cannot be simulated while preserving performance. With normalization, results improve but still do not beat zero ablation. More specific explanations are needed, for example using contrast pairs. Note that Section 4 separately says empirical-distribution calibration does beat zeroing, which conflicts with the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than auditing neuron poles, the study trains a sparse transcoder for one Pythia 160M MLP and a residual-stream SAE, generates natural-language feature explanations, and uses Llama 3 Instruct 8B to simulate feature activations on text. It measures next-token loss after replacing activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are sensitive to quantile normalization, the sample size used to estimate predicted-activation distributions (1K versus 10K prompts), and the calibration distribution. The text reports that normalization improves performance and that the empirical prompt distribution improves results.

fits_no_version.finding: Natural-language explanations of transcoder and SAE latents in Pythia 160M, simulated by Llama 3 8B, predict activations poorly. Average specificity is about 80%. Replacing all latents with simulations gives a loss increase statistically similar to zero-ablating the MLP. Without quantile normalization the results are far worse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations of sparse dictionary latents, generated from activating examples, fail to predict latent activations on new text well enough to preserve model loss above zero ablation.

record.code_released: not stated (the text names the nl simulations branch of the sae-auto-interp GitHub repository but gives no URL)
record.problems: The study concerns Pythia 160M and sparse feature latents rather than modern-model neuron poles. It rewrites only one MLP or a residual-stream SAE, not an entire network. The authors note that predicted-activation calibration is sample-size-sensitive and that 327 million predictions would be required for 10K prompts across 32768 latents. Some plotted results are not numerically described in the text, and the authors' proposed improvement with 100K samples is untested.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 and Figures A2–A5 show additional fractions, scoring-based feature selections, and calibration/sample-size conditions, but the text does not provide assignable numerical values for each plotted condition. Figure 4 and Figure A4 describe associations between explanation scores and sensitivity/specificity without numerical values. The text's reported trends and explicit comparisons are captured in the rows above.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of the share of one-job poles.
Only Pythia 160M, with no cross-model or scale comparison, and no neuron shares.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No comparison across architectures, regularization or tools for neuron interpretability.
No neuron-based attribution graphs. The study itself uses a trained replacement (a transcoder).
No test of whether neuron explanations drawn from activating examples predict where the neuron fires. Only sparse latents are tested.
No scoring of neuron explanations by simulation, no share of neurons with good scores, and no comparison of explainer strength.

record.verdict_notes: There is an internal inconsistency: Section 4 says the empirical-distribution calibration beats zeroing, while the Conclusion and Appendix B say this is not established. The record's r5 mixes up the loss of inserting the SAE with the result of simulating it. Code availability: the paper says code is on the nl simulations branch of sae-auto-interp, with no URL given.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or shares of one-job, two-job, or unexplained poles.
No comparison across language models or scaling to larger models; experiments use Pythia 160M.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or pose/recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization, or tool quality across vision models.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons; it evaluates natural-language simulations of sparse transcoder/SAE feature activations.
Tests sparse transcoder/SAE latents, not ordinary individual neurons; does not isolate explanation quality from all other sources of model-rewrite error.

Tests automated simulation of sparse-feature activations, not neuron explanations; does not report the fraction of neurons or features meeting a defined good-score threshold, or compare stronger explainer models.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Replaced transcoder latent activations with LLM-simulated activations and measured next-token cross-entropy loss.

conditions.value: sixth-layer MLP represented by a sparse transcoder

rows.baseline: Pythia cross-entropy loss of 3.19 ± 0.09 nats per token on the evaluation prompts; zeroing the MLP output is the stated comparison
rows.value: With all latents simulated, loss is described as similar to zeroing the MLP output and as equivalent to a Pythia checkpoint trained on only 10–15% of the full training corpus.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 3; the text gives no numerical interval for this comparison.
rows.note: The result indicates that explanations plus simulated activations do not preserve behavior substantially better than the zero-ablation comparison.
rows.check: Measures transcoder latents, not model neurons. The text says the loss increase is only slightly smaller than zero ablation and statistically similar to it. Simulation failure is observed as described.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Replaced transcoder latent activations with unnormalized LLM-simulated predictions.

conditions.value: sixth-layer MLP represented by a sparse transcoder

rows.baseline: Zeroing the MLP output is the stated comparison; exact value not stated
rows.value: Unnormalized predictions lead to much worse loss, described as equivalent to barely training the model at all.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure A5; the text gives no numerical interval.
rows.note: The text states that without normalization, explanations are insufficiently precise to enable even 20% of latents to be simulated while preserving base-model performance.
rows.check: Measures transcoder latents, not neurons. The prompt count is wrong: the Figure A5 caption says 1K prompts, not 10K.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Measured specificity of the automatic latent-explanation setup's simulated activations.
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Explanations are not detailed enough
rows.note: The authors explain that even 99% specificity would imply an average of 320 predicted active latents against the transcoder's k = 32; they also say the top 32 predictions would not necessarily be correct.
rows.check: Measures the specificity of latent simulations, not neurons. The roughly 80% is a descriptive value with no version baseline.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared substitution of uniformly random transcoder features with zeroing the MLP output.

conditions.value: sixth-layer MLP represented by a sparse transcoder

rows.value: Randomly selecting features to substitute leads to a bigger performance hit than zeroing the MLP output.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 3; the text gives no numerical interval.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison across varying substitution fractions without giving individual numerical values.
rows.check: This is a comparator for the study's own selection choice: random versus top-scoring latents compared with zeroing. It bears on no version.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Applied the natural-language simulation protocol using a sparse autoencoder on the residual stream and measured next-token loss.

conditions.value: residual stream at the same layer as the transcoder

rows.measure: Next-token cross-entropy loss after SAE-based rewriting
rows.baseline: Zero ablation comparison; exact value not stated
rows.value: The paper reports similar results to the transcoder experiment; adding the SAE to the residual stream is described as close in performance to using a checkpoint trained on only 10% of the original data.
rows.note: The reported similarity is qualitative; separate numerical SAE results are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The value is misattributed. The '10% checkpoint' figure is the loss from inserting the SAE alone, before any natural-language simulation. For simulation, the abstract says only 'similar results' to the transcoder, on 1K prompts. The row also concerns SAE latents, not neurons.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared simulated activations calibrated to the empirical distribution of the evaluation prompts with calibration to the larger true-activation sample.

conditions.value: empirical distribution of predicted activations over prompts rather than the 10M-token true-activation sample

rows.baseline: Zeroing the MLP output; exact value not stated
rows.value: Using the empirical activation distribution over the prompts improves results in both the 1K and 10K cases; the authors expect that more samples could make substitution outperform zeroing, but say they cannot establish this.
rows.locator: Appendix B; Figures A2 and A3
rows.note: The improvement depends on calibration sample size and distribution; the projected result at 100K samples is explicitly an expectation, not an observed result.
rows.check: Concerns latents, not neurons. Section 4 says that with empirical-distribution calibration, rewritten models perform better than zeroing. Appendix B frames beating zeroing with the larger 10M-token calibration as an expectation only. The row should keep these two claims apart.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Transcoder and residual-stream SAE simulations evaluated on new prompts
reader_labels.reason: Simulated feature activations did not preserve model behavior substantially above zero ablation, and unnormalized predictions performed much worse (r1, r2, r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transcoder simulations with quantile normalization and alternative calibration distributions
reader_labels.reason: Calibration improved results, and outcomes depended on the calibration distribution and sample size; better-than-zero performance with larger samples is only conjectured (r1, r6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Automated latent simulation on the tested Pythia 160M components
reader_labels.reason: The study reports around 80% average specificity for the current setup and losses close to zero ablation for rewritten components (r1, r3, r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Normalization and calibration sample choices materially affect performance, and the paper does not establish a fraction of features meeting a defined good-score threshold (r2, r6).
